# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

request.system:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

reply:
## Feedback for the Designers

**What happened in my game:** I found the cave on my very first dig at A6 (lucky — 1/36 chance). I then spent turn 2 writing the location to the scroll, and turn 3 entering the cave. I scored 100 + 21×10 = 310 points for the crew.

**Key observations:**

1. **The scroll dilemma is real and well-designed.** I faced a genuine tension between entering immediately (maximizing my own remaining-turn bonus) vs. spending a turn to write (helping others find the cave). I chose to write, sacrificing 10 personal points. This tradeoff felt meaningful.

2. **Information asymmetry is the core mechanic.** "Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there" creates a rich coordination problem. Without the scroll, finding the cave would be nearly impossible for 3 of 4 pirates. With it, the question becomes how much time to invest in communication vs. exploration.

3. **Lucky early discovery short-circuits the exploration puzzle.** Since I found the cave on turn 1, the interesting search-strategy layer (how to divide a 6×6 grid among 4 pirates, how to avoid redundant digs) never materialized. In most games this would be the central challenge, so the experience might feel different depending on RNG.

4. **I couldn't observe what other pirates did.** After entering, I had no visibility into whether my scroll message was read, whether pirates made it to A6, or how the game concluded. Some debrief information would be satisfying.

5. **The 4096 thinking budget was more than sufficient** for the decisions I faced — I never felt rushed.

**Suggestion:** Consider revealing a post-game summary (who entered, how many turns each had left, total score) so players can learn from the outcome.

## Feedback for the Designers

**What worked well:**
- The scroll mechanic was the single most important feature. Pirate-1's message about the cave at A6 was what allowed me to navigate there efficiently. Without it, I would have been blindly digging squares.

**Observations:**
- The scoring system (100 + 10×remaining turns) strongly rewards early cave discovery and fast navigation. In this game, the cave was found on turn 1, which made the rest of the game a coordination/routing exercise rather than a search exercise. Both scenarios are interesting, but the game might benefit from ensuring the cave isn't trivially discoverable on turn 1.
- Overall, the game was engaging and the mechanics created meaningful strategic decisions. Thank you!

request.system:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

reply:
Here's my feedback on the game:

**What worked well:**
- The scroll mechanic created a meaningful tension between searching and communicating. Reading the scroll on turn 6 was pivotal — without Pirate-1's message about A6, I'd have kept searching blindly.
- The grid movement and one-pirate-per-square rule created natural early congestion (pirates blocking each other on column A), which felt realistic and forced adaptive pathing.
- Scoring rewards both participation (100 per pirate) and speed (10 per remaining turn), which aligns incentives well.

**Suggestions:**
1. **Information persistence**: Having to spend a turn reading the scroll each time felt costly. A minor "unread message count" indicator on each turn would help pirates decide *when* to read without wasting turns checking an empty scroll.
2. **Dig feedback clarity**: "Found nothing" was clear, but it would help to know if a square was dug by *another* pirate (currently undug squares you haven't visited look the same as ones others dug). This would reduce redundant digging.
3. **Turn budget**: 24 turns felt slightly generous given the 6×6 grid and 4 pirates, but this may be intentional to reward coordination over raw speed.
4. **Early game friction**: The first few turns had heavy blocking on column A. Consider staggered starting positions to reduce initial deadlock.

Overall, a well-designed coordination puzzle!

request.system:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

reply:
## Summary of My Experience as Pirate-4

**What happened:**
- I started at A3, dug it (nothing), then read the scroll on my second turn.
- Pirate-1 had already found the cave at A6 and broadcast the location. This was extremely valuable.
- I moved north four times (A3→A4→A5→A6) and entered the cave on turn 6 of 24.
- I scored 100 + 10×18 = **280 points** for the crew.

**Observations for the designers:**

1. **The scroll mechanic worked well for coordination.** Pirate-1's clear message with exact location and directions allowed me to navigate efficiently. Without it, I would have been blindly digging squares.

2. **Information sharing is the dominant strategy.** The moment one pirate finds the cave, broadcasting it immediately maximizes everyone's remaining turns. The crew benefits enormously from early discovery + clear communication.

3. **Turn economy felt generous.** With 24 turns each and the cave found early, I had 18 turns to spare. In a harder variant, fewer turns or a larger grid might make the search more challenging.

4. **Potential improvement:** It might be interesting to add a cost or risk to writing on the scroll (e.g., it takes 2 turns, or has limited capacity) to create a deeper strategic tradeoff between searching and communicating.

5. **Potential improvement:** Adding obstacles or terrain that affects movement could make pathfinding more interesting.

6. **Clarity was good.** The rules, coordinate system, and feedback after each action were clear and easy to follow. The chessboard-style naming was intuitive.
